title: Introduction to Logarithms
learningObjective: Convert between exponential and logarithmic form. Evaluate a logarithmic function, including common and natural logarithms.

faqs.question: What is a logarithm, and what question is it actually asking?
faqs.answer:
A logarithm answers the question "what exponent do I need?" Specifically, \( \log_b(x) \) asks: "what power do I have to raise b to, in order to get x?" The logarithm itself IS that exponent — the answer to the question, not some new separate operation you need to memorize from scratch.
Example

\( \log_2(8) \) asks: "2 raised to what power gives 8?"

Since \( 2^3=8 \), the answer is \( \log_2(8)=3 \).

faqs.question: What is the relationship between logarithmic form and exponential form?
faqs.answer:
Every logarithmic equation has an exponential twin that says the exact same thing in different words — they're two notations for one relationship. The base stays the base in both forms; the logarithm's answer becomes the exponent.

\( \log_b(x)=y \) and \( b^y=x \) say exactly the same thing, just arranged differently.

Formula

\[ \log_b(x) = y \iff b^y = x \]

(valid whenever \( b>0 \), \( b \neq 1 \), and \( x>0 \))

faqs.question: What is a common logarithm, and why is it written without a base?
faqs.answer:
A common logarithm is a logarithm with base 10. It comes up often enough that the base is usually left off: in this course and on your calculator's LOG key, log(x) with no base written means log₁₀(x). (Some higher-level math and computer science books use plain log for a different base, so check when you change books.) Your EL3 CheckIt problem writes base 10 out in full, as \( \log_{10} \).
Notation

\[ \log_{10}(x) = \log(x) \]

faqs.question: What is a natural logarithm, and why does it use the special notation ln?
faqs.answer:
A natural logarithm is a logarithm with base e (the same special constant from EL1). It's so common — especially once you reach calculus — that it gets its own unique notation, ln(x), instead of writing log_e(x) every time.
Notation

\[ \log_{e}(x) = \ln(x) \]

faqs.question: How are logarithms and exponential functions related as inverses?
faqs.answer: Extension: the inverse-function view goes beyond the EL3 CheckIt exercise. A logarithmic function undoes what an exponential function does, in the same sense you learned in FN6: if \( f(x)=b^x \) and \( g(x)=\log_b(x) \), then putting an output of \( f \) into \( g \) gives back the original input. Because of this inverse relationship, the domain and range swap: the range of \( f(x)=b^x \), \( (0,\infty) \), is the domain of \( \log_b(x) \), and its domain, all real numbers, is the range of \( \log_b(x) \). (A shifted or reflected exponential can have a different range.)

faqs.question: How do I convert an equation from logarithmic form to exponential form?
faqs.answer:
Identify the base, the logarithm's answer (which becomes the new exponent), and the argument (which becomes the result). Then rewrite using \( b^y=x \).
Worked Example

Convert \( \log_5(25)=2 \) to exponential form.

Base: 5    Answer/exponent: 2    Argument/result: 25

\( 5^2=25 \)

faqs.question: How do I convert an equation from exponential form to logarithmic form?
faqs.answer:
Same process, run in reverse: identify the base, the exponent (which becomes the logarithm's answer), and the result (which becomes the argument). Then rewrite using \( \log_b(x)=y \).
Worked Example

Convert \( 6^3=216 \) to logarithmic form.

Base: 6    Exponent/answer: 3    Result/argument: 216

\( \log_6(216)=3 \)

faqs.question: How do I evaluate a logarithm by inspection, without a calculator?
faqs.answer:
Ask yourself the question from "What is a logarithm?" directly: "what power do I raise the base to, to get this argument?" If you can answer that in your head (or with a little trial and error), you don't need a calculator at all.
Worked Example

Evaluate \( \log_4\left(\dfrac{1}{64}\right) \).

Ask: "4 to what power gives 1/64?"

Since \( 4^{-3}=\dfrac{1}{64} \), the answer is \( -3 \).

faqs.question: How do I evaluate a logarithm that results in a negative number?
faqs.answer:
When the base is greater than 1 (every base on the EL3 CheckIt exercise is), a logarithm is negative exactly when the number inside is strictly between 0 and 1. Here's why: from EL1, a negative exponent makes a reciprocal, so \( b^{-n}=\dfrac{1}{b^n} \), which is less than 1 when \( b>1 \). Working backward, write a number inside like \( \dfrac{1}{81} \) as a power of the base with a negative exponent. Not every fraction gives a negative answer: \( \dfrac{3}{2} \) is bigger than 1, so \( \log_2\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) \) is positive. A negative answer is completely normal and doesn't mean you made a mistake.
Worked Example

Evaluate \( \log_9\left(\dfrac{1}{81}\right) \).

Since \( 81=9^2 \), \( \dfrac{1}{81}=9^{-2} \).

\( \log_9\left(\dfrac{1}{81}\right)=-2 \)

faqs.question: How do I evaluate a common or natural logarithm using a calculator?
faqs.answer:
Extension: the EL3 CheckIt exercise asks only for exact values, so calculator decimals go beyond it. Use the LOG button for common (base 10) logarithms, or the LN button for natural (base e) logarithms — both are standard on any scientific or graphing calculator. Press LOG or LN, type the number inside, close the parenthesis, and press Enter (some older calculators want the number first). The calculator returns a decimal approximation, since most logarithm values aren't clean whole numbers.
Worked Example

\( \log(50) \approx 1.699 \)    \( \ln(50) \approx 3.912 \)

faqs.question: Why must the argument of a logarithm always be positive?
faqs.answer: Extension: domains of log functions go beyond the EL3 CheckIt exercise (you'll use this in EL4). \( \log_b(x)=y \) means \( b^y=x \). With a base \( b>0 \), \( b^y \) is positive for every real \( y \); it never reaches zero or goes negative. So no exponent makes \( b^y \) equal 0 or a negative number, which means \( \log_b(0) \) and the log of a negative number are undefined. The number inside a logarithm must be strictly positive.

faqs.question: How do I find the domain of a logarithmic function like log₃(2x − 4)?
faqs.answer:
Extension: finding a domain goes beyond the EL3 CheckIt exercise (it is part of EL4). Set the argument (everything inside the logarithm) greater than zero, then solve the resulting inequality for x.
Worked Example

Find the domain of \( \log_3(2x-4) \).

Set up the inequality: \( 2x-4 > 0 \)

Solve: \( 2x>4 \) → \( x>2 \)

Domain: \( (2,\infty) \)

Watch the sign: for \( \log_3(6-2x) \), \( 6-2x>0 \) gives \( -2x>-6 \), and dividing by \( -2 \) flips the inequality: \( x<3 \). Domain: \( (-\infty,3) \).

faqs.question: Why do logarithms matter beyond solving exponential equations?
faqs.answer: Extension: these applications go beyond the EL3 CheckIt exercise. Logarithms show up anywhere a quantity spans an enormous range of scale and needs to be compressed into something readable — the Richter scale for earthquakes, decibels for sound, pH for acidity, and star brightness in astronomy are all logarithmic scales. They're also the essential tool for actually solving for a variable that's trapped in an exponent — which becomes one of the most common tasks in the rest of this unit.

guided.title: Understand What a Logarithm Is Asking
guided.prompt: I'm learning what a logarithm means for my EL3 CheckIt. My notes say: log_b(x) = y means b^y = x, so the value of a log is the exponent you put on the base to get the number inside. Give me one logarithm at a time, using only a base from 4 to 10 and a number inside that is that base to the power 2, 3, -2, -3, 1/2 or -1/2 (for example log_7(49) or log_9(3)). Before I evaluate each one, ask me to say the question it asks in words: "the base to what power gives this number?" Don't evaluate it for me. Check my question first, then my answer. After I've done three, explain one new logarithm in words and make one deliberate mistake in your reasoning by asking the question backwards ("what power of the number inside gives the base?"). I'll find it and check it against my notes. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Practice Converting Between Log and Exponential Form
guided.prompt: I'm practicing converting between exponential and logarithmic form for my EL3 CheckIt. My notes say: b^y = x and log_b(x) = y say the same thing; the base stays the base, the exponent is the value of the log, and the result goes inside the log. CheckIt gives equations with two letters and one whole number from 4 to 10, like m^7 = z or log_8(a) = y, and the whole number can be the base, the exponent, or the result. Give me six equations, one at a time: three exponential equations to write in logarithmic form and three logarithmic equations to write in exponential form, with the whole number in a different position each time. For each one, ask me to name the base, the exponent and the result before I write the answer, and don't write the conversion for me. Then convert two new equations yourself, one in each direction, and make one deliberate mistake in one of them by swapping the base and the exponent. I'll find it and read your wrong equation aloud to show why it says something different. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Practice Evaluating Logarithms by Inspection
guided.prompt: I'm practicing evaluating logarithms without a calculator for my EL3 CheckIt. My notes say: to evaluate log_b(x), write x as a power of b; that power is the answer. CheckIt uses bases from 4 to 10 and answers 2, 3, -2, -3, 1/2 and -1/2, and it may print roots in forms like (1/7)sqrt(7) or 2sqrt(2). Give me six logarithms of that kind, one at a time, with at least one of each kind of answer: a positive whole number, a negative whole number, 1/2, and -1/2, and at least one with base 8. Ask me to rewrite the number inside as a power of the base before I give the answer. Don't rewrite it for me; if I'm stuck, ask me a smaller question. Then evaluate two new ones yourself and make one deliberate mistake: drop the negative sign on an answer that should be negative. I'll find it and check it by raising the base to your answer. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Extension: Find the Domain of a Logarithmic Function
guided.prompt: This goes beyond my EL3 CheckIt; it previews EL4. My notes say: log_b(u) is defined only when u > 0 (the number inside must be strictly positive), so the domain of a log function comes from solving "inside > 0". Give me four functions one at a time, each of the form f(x) = log_b(mx + k) with a base b from 2 to 10 and whole numbers m and k, where m is not 0, and use a negative m in at least one of them. For each, ask me to write the inequality, solve it, and give the domain in interval notation. Don't solve it for me. Then solve one more yourself and make one deliberate mistake: write the inequality as "inside >= 0" instead of "inside > 0". I'll find it and explain why the endpoint can't be in the domain by trying to evaluate the log there. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Extension: Check That a Log and an Exponential Are Inverses
guided.prompt: This goes beyond my EL3 CheckIt; it connects EL3 to inverse functions from FN6. My notes say: f and g are inverses when f(g(x)) = x for every x in the domain of g and g(f(x)) = x for every x in the domain of f, and log_b(x) = y means b^y = x. Pick one base b from 2 to 10 and let f(x) = b^x and g(x) = log_b(x). Ask me to compute f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) and to explain each step using the meaning of a log, not a memorized rule. Also ask me which x values each composition works for. Don't compute them for me. Then write your own short check of f(g(x)) = x with one deliberate mistake: say it works for every real number x. I'll find it and use my notes to explain which x values don't work. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

open.title: Create Your Own
open.prompt: Use the AI tool of your choice. Start by describing what you're confused about or curious about from Section EL3 (Introduction to Logarithms). paths.label: EL3: Introduction to Logarithms
paths.intro: Builds to the EL3 check: converting between exponential and logarithmic form, and evaluating logarithms, including common and natural logs. Practice scope: the EL3 CheckIt exercise converts equations made of two letters and one whole number from 4 to 10, and evaluates logs with a base from 4 to 10 whose value is 2, 3, −2, −3, \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) or \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\) (base 10 is written out as \(\log_{10}\)). The ln and no-base log practice and the calculator values in “Common and natural logarithms” go beyond the EL3 CheckIt exercise.

graphs.D0: b is the base in both forms; c, the value of the log, is the exponent; a, the number inside the log, is the result.
graphs.D1: 7 is the base in both forms; 3, the value of the log, is the exponent; 343, the number inside the log, is the result.
graphs.D2: 8 is the base in both forms; 2, the value of the log, is the exponent; 64, the number inside the log, is the result.
graphs.D3: 5 is the base in both forms; 4, the value of the log, is the exponent; 625, the number inside the log, is the result.

stages.desc: Two quick skills EL3 leans on. Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Write numbers as powers
stops.target: Rewrite numbers like \(\tfrac{1}{343}\), \(\sqrt{5}\), and \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) as powers of a base: \(\tfrac{1}{b^n} = b^{-n}\) and \(\sqrt{b} = b^{1/2}\).
stops.cold: Write each as a power: (a) \(\tfrac{1}{343}\) as a power of 7 (b) \(\sqrt{5}\) as a power of 5
stops.coldPlain: Write each as a power: (a) 1/343 as a power of 7, (b) sqrt(5) as a power of 5.
stops.solution: (a) 343 = 7^3, and a reciprocal flips the sign of the exponent: 1/343 = 7^(-3). (b) A square root is the 1/2 power: sqrt(5) = 5^(1/2).
stops.mistake: Writing 1/343 as 7^(1/3), mixing up "reciprocal" (negative exponent) with "root" (fraction exponent).
stops.again: Write each as a power: (a) \(\tfrac{1}{25}\) of 5 (b) \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) of 3 (c) 49 of 7
stops.reflect: What does a negative exponent do? What does a fraction exponent do?

stops.title: Find the missing exponent
stops.target: Solve equations like \(6^x = 216\) by asking "what power of 6 gives 216?"
stops.solution: Count up powers of 6: 6, 36, 216, which is 6^3, so x = 3. For 1/64: 64 = 8^2 and the reciprocal makes the exponent negative, so x = -2.
stops.mistake: Dividing 216 by 6 instead of asking which power.
stops.reflect: This question, "what exponent?", has a name you will learn next. What do you think it is?

stages.desc: What a logarithm means, then one stop per part of the EL3 check, plus common and natural logs from the objective.

stops.title: What a logarithm means
stops.target: \(\log_b a\) is the exponent you put on \(b\) to get \(a\). So \(\log_b a = c\) means exactly the same thing as \(b^c = a\).
stops.explain:
One statement, two forms

A logarithm answers the question "what exponent?" The colors and the caption under the diagram show which piece goes where.

[[graph:D0]]
stops.cold: What is \(\log_7 343\)? Say the question it asks in words.
stops.coldPlain: What is log base 7 of 343? Say the question it asks in words.
stops.solution: Read log base 7 of 343 as "7 to what power gives 343?" 7^3 = 343, so the log is 3. The log is always an exponent.
stops.mistake: Dividing 343 by 7, or thinking log_7 343 means log times 7 times 343.
stops.reflect: Complete the sentence: "A logarithm is an ____."

stops.title: Exponential form to logarithmic form
stops.target: Rewrite \(b^c = a\) as \(\log_b a = c\): the base stays the base, the exponent becomes the value of the log, and the result goes inside the log. This works with letters too.
stops.solution: Base 8 stays the base. The exponent 2 is what the log equals. The result 64 goes inside: log_8 64 = 2.
stops.mistake: Writing log_8 2 = 64 (putting the exponent inside the log).
stops.again: Write in logarithmic form: (a) \(m^7 = z\) (b) \(5^a = b\) (c) \(x^y = 9\)
stops.againA: (a) \(\log_m z = 7\) (b) \(\log_5 b = a\) (c) \(\log_x 9 = y\). Same pattern: base stays, exponent is the answer.
stops.reflect: With letters, how do you decide which letter is the base?
stops.note: For new problems, use two letters and one whole number from 4 to 10, like m^7 = z, as on CheckIt.

stops.title: Logarithmic form to exponential form
stops.target: Rewrite \(\log_b a = c\) as \(b^c = a\): the base stays the base, and the answer to the log becomes the exponent.
stops.solution: The base 5 stays the base; the log value 4 becomes the exponent; the number inside, 625, is the result: 5^4 = 625.
stops.mistake: Writing 625^4 = 5 (the number inside used as the base) or 4^5 = 625 (base and exponent swapped; 4^5 is actually 1024).
stops.again: Write in exponential form: (a) \(\log_p 8 = q\) (b) \(\log_c d = 6\)
stops.reflect: How can you check your conversion by reading it aloud?
stops.note: For new problems, use two letters and one whole number from 4 to 10, like log_8 a = y, as on CheckIt.

stops.title: Evaluate a logarithm
stops.target: Evaluate \(\log_b a\) by writing \(a\) as a power of \(b\); that power is the answer. Answers can be negative or fractions.
stops.solution: Write the number inside as a power of the base. 729 = 9 · 9 · 9 = 9^3 gives 3. 1/25 = 1/5^2 = 5^(-2) gives -2.
stops.mistake: Thinking a log cannot be negative. With a base greater than 1, as on every EL3 CheckIt problem, a negative log just means the number inside is strictly between 0 and 1.
stops.again: Evaluate \(\log_9 3\) and \(\log_7\left(\tfrac{\sqrt{7}}{7}\right)\). (CheckIt may print the second number as \(\tfrac{1}{7}\sqrt{7}\).)
stops.stretch: Evaluate \(\log_8\left(2\sqrt{2}\right)\) and \(\log_8\left(\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\right)\). (CheckIt prints the second number as \(\tfrac{1}{4}\sqrt{2}\).)
stops.stretchA: \(2\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{8} = 8^{1/2}\), so the first is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\). \(\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4} = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{8}} = 8^{-1/2}\), so the second is \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\).
stops.reflect: How does the "Write numbers as powers" stop help here?
stops.note: For new problems, use a base from 4 to 10 and a number inside whose log is 2, 3, -2, -3, 1/2 or -1/2, as on CheckIt.

stops.title: Common and natural logarithms
stops.target: \(\log x\) with no base means base 10 (the common log). \(\ln x\) means base \(e\) (the natural log). Evaluate them exactly when you can, or with a calculator. (Part of the EL3 objective but beyond the EL3 CheckIt exercise, which writes base 10 as \(\log_{10}\) and never uses ln.)
stops.solution: log means base 10: 100 = 10^2, so 2; 0.001 = 1/1000 = 10^(-3), so -3. ln means base e: ln(e^3) asks "e to what power is e^3?", which is 3. For values that are not exact powers, like ln 5, use the calculator: about 1.609. (Calculator values go beyond the EL3 CheckIt exercise, which asks only for exact values.)
stops.mistake: Assuming log with no base means base e, or typing ln when you mean log.
stops.reflect: Which base does each button on your calculator use?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same three-part format as the EL3 CheckIt exercise.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Convert between exponential and logarithmic form, and evaluate a logarithm.
stops.cold:
(a) Write \(a^b = 6\) in logarithmic form.
(b) Write \(\log_x 8 = y\) in exponential form.
(c) Evaluate \(\log_6\left(\tfrac{1}{36}\right)\).
stops.coldPlain: (a) Write a^b = 6 in logarithmic form. (b) Write log_x 8 = y in exponential form. (c) Evaluate log_6 (1/36).
stops.solution: (a) Base a stays; exponent b is the answer; 6 goes inside: log_a 6 = b. (b) Base x stays; y becomes the exponent: x^y = 8. (c) 36 = 6^2, and the reciprocal gives 6^(-2), so the log is -2. The letter b is not always the base: read the positions, not the letters.
stops.mistake: Swapping which letter goes inside the log, or giving +2 in part (c).
stops.again:
(a) Write \(4^c = d\) in logarithmic form.
(b) Write \(\log_9 p = z\) in exponential form.
(c) Evaluate \(\log_{10}\left(\tfrac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\right)\).
stops.againA: (a) \(\log_4 d = c\) (b) \(9^z = p\) (c) \(\tfrac{\sqrt{10}}{10} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} = 10^{-1/2}\), so \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\). CheckIt prints this number as \(\tfrac{1}{10}\sqrt{10}\).
stops.reflect: Which direction of conversion is easier for you, and what will you check on the other one?
stops.note: For new problems, match CheckIt: conversions use two letters and one whole number from 4 to 10; evaluations use a base from 4 to 10 with a value of 2, 3, -2, -3, 1/2 or -1/2.
